etymology: From unaware plus the adverbial -s. Webster 1828: unexpectedly; suddenly; without previous preparation; also, without design or intention. The Authorized Version uses it in both senses, and the difference between them decides two of the most important passages in the law and in the epistles.
biblical_def: Unawares in the KJV runs along two tracks. The first is the manslayer’s: the cities of refuge exist that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares (Numbers 35:11), and Joshua repeats it of the man who kills unawares and unwittingly (Joshua 20:3). Here the word means without intention, and the whole architecture of the six cities rests on the distinction between the murderer and the man whose axe head flew off. God’s law grades guilt by intent and provides a refuge for the one and none for the other. The second track is the church’s danger and it means undetected. Paul warns of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus (Galatians 2:4), and Jude of certain men crept in unawares… turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness (Jude 4). Error does not usually arrive announced. The third use is the sweetest: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2). And our Lord warns that the last day may come upon you unawares (Luke 21:34), which is why the same chapter commands watching.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UNAWARES as unexpectedly; suddenly; at a time when not thought of; also, without design; inadvertently. The KJV uses the second sense of the manslayer and the first of the false teacher and the day of the Lord.
webster_full: UNAWARES, adv. — Unexpectedly; suddenly; at a time when not thought of; without preparation.
Also, without design or intention; inadvertently; as, to injure a man unawares.

Webster’s two senses are exactly the two the Authorized Version employs, and confusing them ruins the law of the cities of refuge. To kill a man at unawares is not to be surprised by it; it is to have had no intention of it.
scriptures: Numbers 35:11
Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
Joshua 20:3
That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood.
Galatians 2:4
And that because of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage:
Hebrews 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Luke 21:34
And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted when the law’s careful distinction between intentional and unintentional bloodshed is flattened — in either direction — and when Galatians 2:4 and Jude 4 are treated as intemperance rather than as apostolic description of how error actually enters a church.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 35 is one of the clearest refutations of the claim that the Mosaic law is indiscriminate. Six cities are appointed, spread through the land, open to the Israelite and to the stranger alike (Numbers 35:15), for the man who killed unawares. The chapter then distinguishes him from the murderer by weapon, by motive, and by prior enmity, and requires a congregation to judge between them. Intent matters to God; so does bloodshed. A modern reading that treats the Old Testament as uniformly harsh has not read this chapter, and a reading that treats intention as the only thing that matters has not read the rest of it — the manslayer still had to flee, and still had to remain until the death of the high priest.

Galatians 2:4 and Jude 4 describe a mechanism, not a mood. False brethren are unawares brought in; ungodly men crept in unawares. Neither apostle imagines heresy arriving with a banner. It comes in through the ordinary doors of hospitality, friendship, and shared vocabulary, which is precisely why Jude and Paul both write to congregations that had not noticed. The remedy Scripture gives is not suspicion of strangers — Hebrews 13:2 forbids that in the same word — but a confessing, watchful eldership that knows what it holds. This is the practical case for a confession of faith: a church that has written down what it believes can tell when something has crept in.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is bishgagah, in error or inadvertently, the standing legal term for unintentional sin; the Greek words in Galatians and Jude mean brought in alongside and slipped in beside.
roots_lines: Hebrew shegagah (H7684) — error, inadvertence; the legal category of unintentional sin and unintentional killing (Numbers 35:11; Joshua 20:3).
Hebrew bibli da'ath — without knowledge; the phrase Joshua 20:3 pairs with it, rendered unwittingly.
Greek pareisaktos (G3920) — brought in alongside, smuggled in; false brethren unawares brought in (Galatians 2:4).
Greek pareisduno (G3921) — to slip in beside, to creep in stealthily; crept in unawares (Jude 4).
Greek lanthano (G2990) — to escape notice; behind entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2).
usage: Which killeth any person at unawares (Numbers 35:11) — the legal category of unintentional bloodshed, for which God appointed refuge.
False brethren unawares brought in (Galatians 2:4) — error enters undetected, through ordinary doors.
Some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2) — the same adverb turned to blessing; hospitality without knowing what is being received.

etymology: From name plus the adverbial ending; Webster 1828: particularly; specially; that is to say. In the Authorized Version it introduces the specification — the general statement has been made, and now the particular is named, whether a city of refuge, a list of nations, or the second great commandment.
biblical_def: Namely is the KJV’s word for moving from the category to the case. God does not leave the cities of refuge as a principle: Namely, Bezer in the wilderness… and Ramoth in Gilead… and Golan in Bashan (Deuteronomy 4:43). The nations to be destroyed are not left vague: namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites (Deuteronomy 20:17). The offering is specified down to the flock: if his offering be of the flocks, namely, of the sheep, or of the goats (Leviticus 1:10). And most weightily, the Lord Jesus uses it to name the second commandment: And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (Mark 12:31). Paul repeats the construction — the whole law is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (Romans 13:9). The habit of the word is worth noticing. Scripture is not content to state duty in the abstract; it names the neighbour, names the nation, names the city, names the animal. Revelation is particular, and a religion that will not descend to particulars is not the religion of the Bible.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NAMELY as particularly; specially; that is to say. It introduces an explanation or specification of what has just been stated in general terms.
webster_full: NAMELY, adv. — Particularly; specially; that is to say.
It is used to introduce a specification or particular enumeration of what has been mentioned generally.
The KJV uses it exactly so, and the effect is cumulative: law, land, sacrifice, and love are each brought down from the category to the named instance.
scriptures: Leviticus 1:10
And if his offering be of the flocks, namely, of the sheep, or of the goats, for a burnt sacrifice; he shall bring it a male without blemish.
Deuteronomy 4:43
Namely, Bezer in the wilderness, in the plain country, of the Reubenites; and Ramoth in Gilead, of the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan, of the Manassites.
Deuteronomy 20:17
But thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee:
Mark 12:31
And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.
Romans 13:9

For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
corruption_summary: The word itself is not contested; the habit it represents is. Scripture’s insistence on naming particulars is resisted wherever love is preached as an atmosphere rather than as a set of named duties toward a named neighbour.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 12:31 is the test case. Our Lord could have said that the second commandment is love; He said namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, and then, when a lawyer tried to keep the neighbour undefined, He answered with a road, a beating, a priest, a Levite, and a Samaritan. The parable is a namely. Preaching that stops at the category — love, compassion, kindness — and never descends to the named person, the named debt, the named quarrel to be reconciled, is preaching Mark 12:31 without the word Christ actually used.

The same instinct guards doctrine. Romans 13:9 lists the commandments by name before summing them, which is the opposite of the modern move that sums first in order to avoid listing. When a church says it holds to love and declines to name what love forbids, the summary has become a way of escaping the particulars it was supposed to gather up. Paul does not permit the escape: the commandments he names are the ones against adultery, murder, theft, false witness, and covetousness, and they are still standing when he has finished summarizing them.
roots_summary: Namely is an English connective supplied by the translators rather than a distinct Hebrew or Greek word; it renders explanatory particles and appositional constructions in both testaments.
roots_lines: English namely — from name plus -ly; Webster 1828, particularly, specially, that is to say.
In the Old Testament it commonly renders the Hebrew waw of explication or a simple apposition, which the translators made explicit for English readers.
In Mark 12:31 the Greek is a demonstrative construction, this, which the KJV expands to namely this to mark the citation of Leviticus 19:18.
In Romans 13:9 the underlying Greek is the article with the quoted commandment; the KJV again supplies namely for clarity.
The translators’ practice of supplying such connectives is the same practice their preface defends, and the italic type of the 1611 marks many of them.
usage: Namely, Bezer in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 4:43) — mercy given an address; the cities of refuge are named, not described.
Namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (Mark 12:31) — the second commandment stated, not merely alluded to.
Briefly comprehended in this saying, namely (Romans 13:9) — a summary that names its contents rather than replacing them.

etymology: From some plus what. Webster 1828 gives both a noun sense — something, more or less — and an adverbial one, in some degree. The KJV keeps the noun, now nearly extinct in English: I have somewhat to say unto thee means I have a thing to say, not I have a little to say.
biblical_def: The KJV’s somewhat is usually a noun, and mistaking it for the modern adverb weakens some of the most serious sentences in Scripture. When our Lord says to His host, Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee (Luke 7:40), He is not softening the blow; He has a matter to lay before him, and the parable of the two debtors follows. When the risen Christ says to Ephesus, Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love (Revelation 2:4), He is not registering mild dissatisfaction. He has a charge. The Old Testament uses it the same way for guilt incurred unawares: When a ruler hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance against any of the commandments of the LORD his God… and is guilty (Leviticus 4:22). Two other uses are worth keeping. Rehoboam’s petitioners ask him to ease somewhat the grievous servitude (2 Chronicles 10:4), where the adverbial sense of degree is genuine. And Paul says of the Jerusalem leaders who seemed to be somewhat that God accepteth no man's person (Galatians 2:6) — to be somewhat is to be somebody, and Paul declines to weigh reputation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives SOMEWHAT as a noun — something, more or less; a certain quantity or degree — and as an adverb, in some degree or quantity. The KJV’s commonest use is the noun, which modern English has almost entirely lost.
webster_full: SOMEWHAT, n. — Something, though uncertain what; more or less; a certain quantity or degree, indeterminate.
Also, a person or thing of some importance; as, he thinks himself somewhat.
SOMEWHAT, adv. — In some degree or quantity; as, somewhat larger.

Both senses stand in the KJV. Luke 7:40 and Revelation 2:4 are the noun — a matter, a charge; 2 Chronicles 10:4 is the adverb of degree; and Galatians 2:6 is Webster’s second noun sense, a person of reputed importance.
scriptures: Leviticus 4:22
When a ruler hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance against any of the commandments of the LORD his God concerning things which should not be done, and is guilty;
Luke 7:40
And Jesus answering said unto him, Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee. And he saith, Master, say on.
Revelation 2:4
Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
Galatians 2:6
But of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me:
2 Chronicles 10:4
Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father, and his heavy yoke that he put upon us, and we will serve thee.
corruption_summary: The corruption is a misreading with real consequences: taking the noun for the adverb turns Christ’s charge against Ephesus into a mild complaint, and turns Leviticus 4:22 from guilt into a trifle.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 2:4 is the verse that suffers most. Read as the modern adverb, I have somewhat against thee sounds like a minor reservation appended to a commendation, and it is preached that way — a church doing well with a small area for growth. The English of 1611 will not carry that. Christ has a matter against Ephesus, and the following verse gives the sentence: Repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place. That is the removal of a church, and it is what the somewhat introduces. A church that has kept its doctrine, its discipline, and its patience, and lost its first love, is under a threat, not a suggestion.

Leviticus 4:22 loses in the other direction. A ruler who hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance is guilty — the text says so in the same sentence. Ignorance reduces neither the fact nor the need for a sacrifice; it only changes which offering is brought. The modern instinct that sincerity cancels culpability has no footing here. Guilt in Scripture is a status before God’s law, not a feeling about one’s own conduct, and Leviticus 4 exists precisely because a man can incur it without noticing.
roots_summary: Somewhat is an English word, not the rendering of a single Hebrew or Greek lemma; it stands for indefinite pronouns and neuter substantives in both testaments.
roots_lines: English somewhat — Webster 1828, something, more or less; also a person of reputed importance.
Greek ti (G5100) — the indefinite something; behind I have somewhat to say unto thee (Luke 7:40) and I have somewhat against thee (Revelation 2:4).
Greek einai ti — to be something, that is, to be somebody; Galatians 2:6, and compare Galatians 6:3, if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing.
Hebrew 'achath in Leviticus 4:22 is the ordinary one or any one of the commandments; the KJV renders the sense with somewhat.
The modern narrowing of somewhat to a degree-adverb happened after 1611 and is the source of the misreading.
usage: Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee (Luke 7:40) — a matter to lay before a man, not a small remark.
I have somewhat against thee (Revelation 2:4) — a charge from the risen Christ, answered in the next verse with a threat to remove the candlestick.
Who seemed to be somewhat (Galatians 2:6) — to be somebody; Paul refuses to weigh reputation because God accepts no man's person.

etymology: From all plus together. Webster 1828: wholly; completely; without exception. In the Authorized Version it is the adverb of totality, and it is applied to the smoke on Sinai, to the judgments of the LORD, to God’s knowledge of a man’s words, and to Paul’s wish for his hearers.
biblical_def: Altogether in the KJV means entirely, without remainder, and Scripture reserves it for places where a partial statement would be false. The judgments of the LORD are true and righteous altogether (Psalm 19:9) — not mostly righteous, not righteous on balance. There is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether (Psalm 139:4) — the divine knowledge of a man’s speech has no gaps in it. Mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke (Exodus 19:18), the whole mountain, not a summit. Deuteronomy makes it the measure of justice: That which is altogether just shalt thou follow (Deuteronomy 16:20). The word also exposes men. The blind man’s accusers dismiss him: Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? (John 9:34) — a true statement about every man, used as a slander against one. And Paul, in chains before Agrippa, gives the word its warmest use in Scripture: I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds (Acts 26:29). He wants their whole conversion, and he does not want his chains for them.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALTOGETHER as wholly; entirely; completely; without exception. It is the adverb of totality, and the KJV uses it where anything less than the whole would misstate the case.
webster_full: ALTOGETHER, adv. — Wholly; entirely; completely; without exception.
Also, conjointly; in company; all in one body — though this sense is now expressed by all together, written separately.
Both senses appear in the KJV. Psalm 19:9 and Psalm 139:4 are the adverb of completeness; Job 13:5, O that ye would altogether hold your peace, carries the sense of all of them together.
scriptures: Exodus 19:18
And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly.
Psalm 19:9
The fear of the LORD is clean, enduring for ever: the judgments of the LORD are true and righteous altogether.
Psalm 139:4
For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.
John 9:34
They answered and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out.
Acts 26:29
And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted by subtraction: whenever Scripture’s totalities are read as generalities — God’s judgments righteous in the main, His knowledge of us broad but not exhaustive, conversion substantial but not entire.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 139:4 is one of the plainest statements of exhaustive divine knowledge in the Old Testament, and the word that makes it exhaustive is altogether. Open theism — the position of Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders that God does not know the free future exhaustively — requires this verse and its neighbours to mean something less than they say. But the psalm has already ruled that out: God knows the word before it is on the tongue, understands the thought afar off, and compasses the path and the lying down. To say that God knows a man’s speech altogether is to deny that there is any part of it He does not know, which is what the Reformed doctrine of omniscience has always confessed and what open theism was invented to avoid.

Acts 26:29 marks the second corruption, which is the acceptance of almost. Agrippa’s almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian is one of the saddest lines in the book, and Paul answers it by asking God for the whole thing: both almost, and altogether. A gospel that is content to leave men impressed, interested, and unconverted has settled for what Paul refused. The Puritans wrote whole treatises on the almost-Christian for this reason, and the doctrine behind it is monergistic: no man is altogether such as Paul except by the effectual call, which is why Paul prays for it rather than merely urging it.
roots_summary: Altogether is an English adverb of totality rendering several Hebrew and Greek expressions of wholeness — the Hebrew adverb yachad or an emphatic construction, and in the New Testament words meaning wholly or in great measure.
roots_lines: English altogether — Webster 1828, wholly, entirely, completely, without exception.
Hebrew yachad (H3162) — together, alike, all at once; behind the totality in Psalm 19:9 and Job 13:5.
Hebrew kullah — the whole of it; the force behind mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke (Exodus 19:18).
Greek holos (G3650) — whole, entire; thou wast altogether born in sins (John 9:34).
Greek en megalo in Acts 26:29 — in much, set against in little; the KJV’s almost, and altogether renders the contrast exactly.
usage: True and righteous altogether (Psalm 19:9) — no clause of God’s judgments is exempt from the verdict.
Thou knowest it altogether (Psalm 139:4) — exhaustive divine knowledge of a man’s speech.
Both almost, and altogether such as I am (Acts 26:29) — Paul refuses to be content with an impressed hearer.

etymology: Archaic third-person singular of belong, formed with the -eth ending standard in the Authorized Version. Webster 1828 defines BELONG as to be the property of; to be the concern or proper business of; to be appendant to. In the KJV the word settles questions of ownership — of land, of office, and above all of vengeance and of power.
biblical_def: Belongeth answers the question whose is it? and in the KJV that question is usually settled against us. To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence (Deuteronomy 32:35) — the verse Paul and Hebrews both quote to take the sword out of the believer’s hand. God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God (Psalm 62:11) — not chiefly, not derivatively, but as His own. The word also assigns duty and place. This is it that belongeth unto the Levites: from twenty and five years old and upward they shall go in to wait upon the service of the tabernacle (Numbers 8:24) — the office has an owner and an age. Towns belong to tribes: Gibeah belongeth to Benjamin (Judges 19:14), Shochoh belongeth to Judah (1 Samuel 17:1), Zarephath belongeth to Zidon (1 Kings 17:9), where God sends His prophet to be fed by a Gentile widow. And the New Testament applies it to maturity: strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil (Hebrews 5:14). Every use draws a line of ownership, and the lines are God’s to draw.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BELONG as to be the property of; to be the concern or proper business of; to be appendant or related to. BELONGETH is the archaic third-person singular retained throughout the Authorized Version.
webster_full: BELONG, v.i. — To be the property of; as, the house belongs to the man.
To be the concern or proper business of; to appertain; as, it belongs to the magistrate to judge.
To be appendant to; to be connected with; to have relation to.
Webster’s three senses map the biblical uses: property (Psalm 62:11), proper business or office (Numbers 8:24; Hebrews 5:14), and appurtenance of place (Judges 19:14).
scriptures: Numbers 8:24
This is it that belongeth unto the Levites: from twenty and five years old and upward they shall go in to wait upon the service of the tabernacle of the congregation:
Deuteronomy 32:35
To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
Psalm 62:11
God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God.
1 Kings 17:9
Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee.
Hebrews 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
corruption_summary: The corruption is theft of what belongs to God — vengeance taken into private hands, and power treated as a human possession to be seized, negotiated, or distributed rather than received.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 32:35 is quoted twice in the New Testament for one purpose: to stop a Christian avenging himself. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord (Romans 12:19), and again at Hebrews 10:30. The prohibition is not a counsel of niceness; it is a property claim. Vengeance belongs to God, and the believer who takes it has stolen. Scripture does not thereby abolish justice — the magistrate beareth not the sword in vain (Romans 13:4), and the state is God’s appointed avenger — but it removes the sword from the offended man’s own hand. The distinction between personal retaliation and civil justice is exactly the distinction the modern age blurs in both directions.

Psalm 62:11 answers the age’s theory of power. If power belongs to God, then every human authority holds it on loan and answers for its use, and no framework that treats power as the fundamental social reality — something groups possess, seize, or are denied — can be adopted as an explanation of the world. Scripture’s categories for injustice are sin, the fallen heart, covenant-breaking, and the oppression of the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the stranger, all of which name real wrongs and name them before God. The believer’s comfort in the psalm is that the same verse which humbles the powerful assures the weak: the power in question is not finally in the hands of the men who are using it against them.
roots_summary: The Hebrew has no single verb to belong; possession is expressed with the preposition le, to or for. Deuteronomy 32:35 is literally to me vengeance, and the KJV supplies the verb.
roots_lines: English -eth — the third-person singular ending standard in 1611 and retained throughout the Authorized Version.
Hebrew le (the lamed preposition) — to, for, belonging to; Deuteronomy 32:35 reads to me vengeance and recompence.
Hebrew naqam (H5359) — vengeance; the noun God claims as His own in Deuteronomy 32:35.
Hebrew 'oz (H5797) — strength, power; power belongeth unto God (Psalm 62:11).
Greek esti with the genitive in Hebrews 5:14 — is of the full-grown; the KJV renders the genitive of possession with belongeth.
usage: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence (Deuteronomy 32:35) — quoted at Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30 to disarm the believer.
Power belongeth unto God (Psalm 62:11) — heard twice because said once; the ground of both humility and comfort.
Strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age (Hebrews 5:14) — maturity earns its diet by use, not by age alone.

etymology: Older spelling of entreated, from Old French entraiter, to treat with or petition. Webster 1828: ENTREAT, to ask earnestly; to beseech; to supplicate. The KJV’s intreated runs in two directions — a man intreats the LORD, and the LORD is intreated of him, which is the Authorized Version’s way of saying that the prayer was heard and granted.
biblical_def: The great feature of intreated in the KJV is its passive: God is intreated of men. And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren: and the LORD was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived (Genesis 25:21) — the same verb on both sides of the sentence, the asking and the granting joined. Moses, who has every reason to be done with Pharaoh, went out from Pharaoh, and intreated the LORD (Exodus 8:30; 10:18). Manoah intreated the LORD for instruction about the child to be born (Judges 13:8). After the plague David built an altar, so the LORD was intreated for the land, and the plague was stayed from Israel (2 Samuel 24:25). Even Manasseh — the worst king Judah had — prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom (2 Chronicles 33:13). Ezra records the same after a fast: we fasted and besought our God for this: and he was intreated of us (Ezra 8:23). The New Testament turns the word toward Christian character: the wisdom from above is easy to be intreated (James 3:17), that is, approachable, open to appeal, not hardened against a petition.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ENTREAT as to ask earnestly; to beseech; to supplicate; to importune. The archaic passive to be intreated of means to be prevailed upon by petition — which the KJV uses of God granting prayer.
webster_full: ENTREAT, v.t. — To ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition or pray with urgency; to supplicate; to importune.
To be entreated — to be prevailed on by petition or supplication.
Also, in older English, to treat or deal with in a certain manner; as, they entreated him shamefully (Luke 20:11).
The passive is the theological word. That God was intreated does not mean He was worn down; it means He had appointed prayer as the means and honoured it.
scriptures: Genesis 25:21
And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren: and the LORD was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
Exodus 8:30
And Moses went out from Pharaoh, and intreated the LORD.
2 Samuel 24:25
And David built there an altar unto the LORD, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD was intreated for the land, and the plague was stayed from Israel.
2 Chronicles 33:13
And prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD he was God.
James 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
corruption_summary: The passive the LORD was intreated is corrupted in two opposite directions: by those who read it as God changing His mind under pressure, and by those who so guard His immutability that prayer becomes a private exercise with no real appointment as a means.
corruption_paragraphs: The first error is the open-theist reading, which takes the LORD was intreated of him as evidence that God’s purposes are genuinely revisable and His knowledge of the future incomplete. Scripture does not permit it. God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent (Numbers 23:19), and I am the LORD, I change not (Malachi 3:6). The same God who decreed that Rebekah should conceive decreed that Isaac should pray for it, and the text records both without embarrassment. That God ordains ends together with means is the Reformed answer, and it is not a dodge; it is what Genesis 25:21 actually shows, with the asking and the granting expressed by one verb.

The second error over-corrects. If nothing can move God, why pray? The answer of the confession is that prayer is a means God has appointed and honours, not a lever that moves Him. Manasseh is the proof at the extreme end: an idolater who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, who in affliction prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him (2 Chronicles 33:13). No sinner is beyond the reach of that passive verb. James 3:17 then makes the character consequence explicit — the wisdom from above is easy to be intreated. A God who hears petitions makes a people who can be appealed to, and an unapproachable Christian has not imitated Him but contradicted Him.
roots_summary: The Hebrew verb is 'athar, to pray or supplicate, whose passive form means to be supplicated and to grant. The Greek in James is a compound meaning easily persuaded or open to appeal.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'athar (H6279) — to pray, entreat; in the passive (niphal), to be entreated, to grant a petition (Genesis 25:21; 2 Samuel 24:25; 2 Chronicles 33:13; Ezra 8:23).
The KJV’s repetition of one English verb in Genesis 25:21 mirrors the Hebrew, which uses the same root actively and passively in a single verse.
Greek eupeithes (G2138) — easily persuaded, compliant, open to appeal; easy to be intreated (James 3:17).
The older English spelling intreat for entreat is standard in 1611 and retained in most KJV printings.
A separate older sense of the same English verb means to treat or handle — entreated him shamefully (Luke 20:11) — and should not be confused with petition.
usage: Isaac intreated the LORD… and the LORD was intreated of him (Genesis 25:21) — asking and granting in one verb; twenty years of praying answered in one line.
He was intreated of him (2 Chronicles 33:13) — said of Manasseh, which sets the outer limit of what repentance may hope for.
Easy to be intreated (James 3:17) — a mark of heavenly wisdom; approachability as a Christian duty, not a temperament.

etymology: From Old French a part, to the side. Webster 1828: separately; at a distance; aside. The KJV uses it for three distinct separations — the holy setting apart of what belongs to God, the ceremonial putting apart of the unclean, and the physical withdrawal of a man or a company from the crowd.
biblical_def: Apart in Scripture marks a line drawn, and everything depends on who draws it and why. First, God sets apart: Thou shalt set apart unto the LORD all that openeth the matrix (Exodus 13:12), and, more sweetly, know that the LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the LORD will hear when I call unto him (Psalm 4:3). Election and consecration are both in that verb. Second, the law puts apart the ceremonially unclean: a woman shall be put apart seven days (Leviticus 15:19), and the same term governs Leviticus 18:19 — a separation that teaches Israel there are states in which a man may not simply proceed as usual into the presence of God. Third, the word marks withdrawal for grief or for prayer. Zechariah’s picture of national mourning is a nation broken into families, each grieving alone: every family apart… and their wives apart (Zechariah 12:12-13). Our Lord took Peter, James, and John up into an high mountain apart (Matthew 17:1) for the transfiguration. And James turns it into a command: Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word (James 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives APART as separately; at a distance; aside; also, in a state of separation as to place or purpose. The biblical senses — set apart to God, put apart as unclean, withdrawn from the company — are all Webster’s.
webster_full: APART, adv. — Separately; at a distance; in a state of separation as to place.
Aside; in exclusion of the rest; as, to set apart for a particular use.
Also, distinctly, or by itself; as, to consider a thing apart from its consequences.
The moral weight comes from what the separation is for. To be set apart unto the LORD is consecration; to be put apart for uncleanness is exclusion; to go apart with Christ is discipleship.
scriptures: Exodus 13:12
That thou shalt set apart unto the LORD all that openeth the matrix, and every firstling that cometh of a beast which thou hast; the males shall be the LORD'S.
Psalm 4:3
But know that the LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the LORD will hear when I call unto him.
Leviticus 15:19
And if a woman have an issue, and her issue in her flesh be blood, she shall be put apart seven days: and whosoever toucheth her shall be unclean until the even.
Matthew 17:1
And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart,
James 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
corruption_summary: Apart is corrupted when separation unto God is collapsed into separation from people — withdrawal made a virtue in itself — and when the setting apart of Psalm 4:3 is read as a man’s achievement rather than the LORD’s act.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 4:3 is a monergistic sentence and it is regularly read as a moralistic one. The KJV is precise: the LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself. The setting apart is God’s work, the possession is God’s own, and the assurance that follows — the LORD will hear when I call unto him — rests on that fact and not on the psalmist’s performance. Read the other way round, as though a man made himself godly and thereby earned separation, the verse becomes a treadmill. Unconditional election is not a doctrine imported into this psalm; it is the grammar of it.

The second corruption is separation as an end. Christ took the three apart up the mountain, and then brought them straight down into a crowd and a demoniac boy. Withdrawal in Scripture is always for the sake of return — to pray, to be taught, to mourn, and then to go back. The monastic instinct that makes withdrawal itself the higher life, and its modern Protestant cousin that treats a private spirituality as superior to the visible church, both mistake the pattern. So does the reverse error of a Christian who never goes apart at all. James 1:21 gives the only separation that is unqualified and permanent: lay apart all filthiness. Sin is the one thing a believer is told to leave and never rejoin.
roots_summary: Several words lie behind the English. The Hebrew badal and 'abar govern the setting apart of the firstborn; niddah stands behind the ceremonial putting apart; and the Greek kat' idian and apotithemi carry the New Testament senses.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abar (H5674) — to cause to pass over, to devote; behind set apart unto the LORD all that openeth the matrix (Exodus 13:12).
Hebrew palah (H6395) — to distinguish, to set apart; the LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself (Psalm 4:3).
Hebrew niddah (H5079) — separation, impurity; the ceremonial putting apart of Leviticus 15:19 and 18:19.
Greek kat' idian — privately, by themselves; up into an high mountain apart (Matthew 17:1).
Greek apotithemi (G659) — to put off, lay aside as a garment; lay apart all filthiness (James 1:21).
usage: Set apart unto the LORD (Exodus 13:12) — consecration; the firstborn are removed from common use.
The LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself (Psalm 4:3) — God’s act, God’s possession, and the ground of confidence in prayer.
Lay apart all filthiness (James 1:21) — the one separation with no return; sin is put off like a garment before the word is received.

etymology: Old English beneothan, below. Webster 1828: under; lower in place; also, lower in rank, dignity, or excellence. In the Authorized Version it draws the vertical axis of the universe — heaven above, earth beneath, the water under the earth — and our Lord uses it to divide two orders of men.
biblical_def: Beneath in Scripture is first cosmological and then moral. The second commandment maps the whole created order with it: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth (Exodus 20:4). Nothing in any tier of creation may be made into an image of God, which is the point of the exhaustive survey. Deuteronomy repeats the tiers when it forbids the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth (Deuteronomy 4:18). The tabernacle uses the word technically, of boards coupled together beneath at the corners (Exodus 26:24) and of the brasen grate under the compass of the altar beneath unto the midst of it (Exodus 38:4). Then the Lord Jesus takes the vertical axis and makes it a division of persons: Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world (John 8:23). That is not geography. It is origin, nature, and destiny, and it is the plainest statement in the Gospels that the difference between Christ and unbelieving men is not degree but source.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BENEATH as under; lower in place; and figuratively, lower in rank, dignity, or excellence — also, unworthy of, as beneath a man’s notice. The KJV uses the literal sense throughout and the figurative in John 8:23.
webster_full: BENEATH, prep. — Under; lower in place, with something directly over or on; as, the earth beneath our feet.
Lower in rank, dignity or excellence; as, brutes are beneath man.
Unbecoming; unworthy of; as, an action beneath a gentleman.
BENEATH, adv. — In a lower place; below, as opposed to heaven or to any thing above.
Webster’s adverbial gloss — below, as opposed to heaven — is precisely the contrast our Lord draws in John 8:23.
scriptures: Exodus 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Deuteronomy 4:18
The likeness of any thing that creepeth on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth:
Exodus 26:24
And they shall be coupled together beneath, and they shall be coupled together above the head of it unto one ring: thus shall it be for them both; they shall be for the two corners.
Exodus 38:4
And he made for the altar a brasen grate of network under the compass thereof beneath unto the midst of it.
John 8:23
And he said unto them, Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world.
corruption_summary: John 8:23 is corrupted whenever the division between from beneath and from above is softened into a difference of maturity, temperament, or spiritual journey rather than a difference of origin and nature.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord’s sentence admits no middle tier. Ye are from beneath; I am from above is spoken to religious men, not to obvious reprobates, and it locates the problem below their behaviour, in their source. The doctrine is total depravity and the necessity of the new birth: Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). Preaching that treats the unconverted as Christians at an earlier stage — further back on the same road — has erased the vertical line John 8:23 draws. There is no gradual ascent from beneath to above; there is a birth from above, and it is God’s to give.

The second commandment’s use of the word guards a related truth. God forbids the likeness of anything in heaven above, in the earth beneath, or in the water under the earth — the survey is exhaustive precisely because human ingenuity is. Every tier of creation has been tried as material for an image, and every one is refused. Where the modern instinct wants a God who can be pictured, felt, and localized — whether in a statue, an experience, or a screen — Exodus 20:4 has already ruled on the whole class. The regulative principle of worship stands on this verse: God is to be worshipped as He has commanded, and no image of any tier of creation may stand in for Him.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is tachath, under or beneath, the ordinary preposition of what lies below; the Greek in John 8:23 is kato, below, set against ano, above.
roots_lines: Hebrew tachath (H8478) — under, beneath, in place of; the ordinary preposition of position below (Exodus 20:4; Deuteronomy 4:18).
Hebrew mattah (H4295) — downward, beneath; used of the lower part of a structure (Exodus 26:24; 38:4).
Greek kato (G2736) — below, downward; ye are from beneath (John 8:23).
Greek ano (G507) — above; the contrasting term in the same verse and in Colossians 3:1-2, seek those things which are above.
The threefold cosmology of Exodus 20:4 — heaven above, earth beneath, water under the earth — is a merism for the whole creation, not a scientific diagram.
usage: In the earth beneath (Exodus 20:4) — one tier of an exhaustive survey; no part of creation may be made an image of God.
Coupled together beneath (Exodus 26:24) — the technical builder’s sense in the tabernacle.
Ye are from beneath; I am from above (John 8:23) — origin, not degree; the line the new birth crosses.

etymology: From a- plus loud. Webster 1828: loudly; with a strong voice or great noise. In the Authorized Version it belongs chiefly to two activities — praise and prophetic warning — and in both the volume is commanded rather than merely permitted.
biblical_def: Aloud in Scripture is not enthusiasm but obedience; God repeatedly commands audible worship and audible warning. The psalms are full of it: Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob (Psalm 81:1); I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning (Psalm 59:16); my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness (Psalm 51:14, David’s vow after his sin); let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds (Psalm 149:5). It is also the volume of prayer under pressure: Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice (Psalm 55:17). And it is the prophet’s commission: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins (Isaiah 58:1) — where the volume and the content are commanded together, and the content is sin named to the people who are committing it. Job’s complaint is the other side of it: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment (Job 19:7). The word assumes a God who hears and a congregation that can be heard.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALOUD as loudly; with a loud voice or great noise. The KJV uses it of singing, of crying to God in prayer, and of the prophet’s public rebuke.
webster_full: ALOUD, adv. — Loudly; with a loud voice, or great noise.
The word implies audibility to others, not merely volume; to cry aloud is to be heard by those present.
That is why Isaiah 58:1 pairs it with a trumpet. The prophet’s rebuke is not a private conviction but a public declaration that the people cannot claim they did not hear.
scriptures: Psalm 51:14
Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.
Psalm 55:17
Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.
Psalm 81:1
To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of Asaph. Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob.
Isaiah 58:1
Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.
Job 19:7
Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment.
corruption_summary: The corruption is on both sides of the volume: congregational praise reduced to a performance the people watch in silence, and prophetic rebuke muted into inoffensiveness so that Isaiah 58:1 is obeyed in neither its loudness nor its content.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 81:1 and Psalm 149:5 assume a people who sing. Congregational psalmody was one of the Reformation’s recoveries precisely because the medieval church had moved the singing from the pews to the choir, and it is worth noticing how easily that reverses. Where the volume comes from the platform and the congregation listens, the command to sing aloud unto God our strength is being performed on the people’s behalf rather than obeyed by them. The regulative principle bears on this: God has commanded His people to sing, and a service arranged so that they need not is not more reverent but less obedient.

Isaiah 58:1 is the harder half. The command is to cry aloud, to spare not, to sound like a trumpet, and to shew my people their transgression — and the people in view are God’s own, in the middle of a fast they think is going well. Preaching that has decided in advance never to name a sin its hearers actually commit has kept the volume and lost the commission, or more often lost both. The prophet is not licensed to be cruel; the chapter goes on to promise light rising in obscurity and a rebuilt city. But the promise comes after the naming, and no amount of warmth later excuses silence now.
roots_summary: The English adverb renders Hebrew expressions of loud voice — commonly ranan, to give a ringing cry, and the phrase begaron, with the throat, in Isaiah 58:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew ranan (H7442) — to give a ringing cry, to shout for joy; behind sing aloud in Psalm 51:14, 59:16, and 81:1.
Hebrew qara' begaron — literally call with the throat; Isaiah 58:1, rendered cry aloud.
Hebrew shophar (H7782) — the trumpet Isaiah names as the standard of the prophet’s volume.
Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, roar, be in tumult; behind the crying aloud of Psalm 55:17.
The KJV distinguishes crying aloud from crying out; the first is deliberate publication, the second often distress.
usage: Sing aloud unto God our strength (Psalm 81:1) — congregational praise commanded, not merely allowed.
Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud (Psalm 55:17) — fixed hours and an audible voice.
Cry aloud, spare not… shew my people their transgression (Isaiah 58:1) — the volume and the content commanded in one breath.

etymology: Comparative of bad or ill, from Old English wyrsa. Webster 1828: more bad, or more evil; less good. In the Authorized Version it is chiefly the historians’ verdict on successive generations, and the New Testament’s verdict on apostasy and on neglect of one’s own household.
biblical_def: Worse is the word Scripture uses when a generation has taken what it received and made it lower. Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him (1 Kings 16:25). Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel (2 Chronicles 33:9) — the covenant nation outdoing the nations it had displaced. Jeremiah says it twice of his own contemporaries: they did worse than their fathers (Jeremiah 7:26), and ye have done worse than your fathers (Jeremiah 16:12). Decline is not automatic in Scripture, but it is common, and the prophets treat each generation as responsible for it. The New Testament sharpens the word. Peter says of those who escape the world’s pollutions through knowledge of Christ and are entangled again, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning (2 Peter 2:20). Paul says that a man who provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house… is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8). And Paul rebukes a church whose gatherings had begun to harm it: ye come together not for the better, but for the worse (1 Corinthians 11:17).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WORSE as more bad or more evil; less good; and, of health, more sick. It is the comparative of ill, and the KJV uses it as a moral and covenantal verdict rather than a mere measure of degree.
webster_full: WORSE, a. — More bad or more evil; less good; inferior in goodness or quality.
In a state of health, more sick; as, the patient is worse.
WORSE, adv. — In a manner more evil or bad; as, they did worse than their fathers.
Webster’s adverbial illustration is itself a paraphrase of Jeremiah, which shows how thoroughly the biblical idiom had entered the English of his day.
scriptures: 1 Kings 16:25
But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him.
2 Chronicles 33:9
So Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel.
Jeremiah 16:12
And ye have done worse than your fathers; for, behold, ye walk every one after the imagination of his evil heart, that they may not hearken unto me:
2 Peter 2:20

For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.
1 Timothy 5:8
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted by the modern assumption of progress — that later is by definition better — and by the therapeutic instinct that will not permit a comparative moral verdict on a generation, a church, or a man at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture’s historians are perfectly willing to say that a generation is worse than the one before it, and to name the men responsible. Jeremiah 16:12 does not hedge: ye have done worse than your fathers, and the reason given is that each man walks after the imagination of his evil heart. The reigning assumption of the last two centuries is the reverse — that the arc of history bends upward and that later opinion is by that fact more enlightened. Where that assumption governs, 2 Chronicles 33:9 becomes unreadable, because it says a covenant people can sink below the pagans they replaced. The Chronicler’s verdicts are this dictionary’s verdicts. Faithful kings are named faithful; apostate kings are named apostate; and generations are measured against the light they were given.

1 Timothy 5:8 and 2 Peter 2:20 are the two comparatives that fall on individuals, and both are severe. A man who will not provide for his own household is worse than an infidel — worse, that is, than a man who makes no Christian profession at all, because the unbeliever generally still feeds his children. And the apostate who has known the way of righteousness and turned from it is in a worse state than before he knew it. Neither verse can be softened into a comment on someone’s difficulties. They are the New Testament’s warning that light received raises the stakes, and that a profession abandoned leaves a man lower than where it found him.
roots_summary: The Hebrew idiom is to do evil more than those before; the Greek uses ordinary comparatives of bad and worse. The English comparative renders both without a distinct lemma of its own.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to be evil, to do wickedly; the comparative is formed with min, more than (1 Kings 16:25; Jeremiah 16:12).
Greek cheiron (G5501) — worse; the latter end is worse with them than the beginning (2 Peter 2:20) and the rent is made worse (Matthew 9:16).
Greek apistos (G571) — unbelieving, an infidel; the standard against which the neglectful provider is measured (1 Timothy 5:8).
Greek hesson (G2276) — less, worse; not for the better, but for the worse (1 Corinthians 11:17).
The Chronicler’s comparative verdicts on the kings are a fixed literary device, not a rhetorical exaggeration.
usage: Did worse than all that were before him (1 Kings 16:25) — the historian’s verdict on a king, stated plainly.
The latter end is worse with them than the beginning (2 Peter 2:20) — apostasy leaves a man lower than it found him.
Worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8) — the provider who neglects his own house measured against a man with no profession at all.
